answer: Yes. When you create a TOM with `add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>`, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created along with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; applicable only to TOMs on CHM7 cards). Example: `add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD`. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show tom-type-<tom-type> support-third-party-toms`. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false, true) that states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The same command also returns description (string 0..255), data-rate (uint16, Gbps), and generic-subtype, which is the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. `show tom-type` with no AID lists all supported TOM types. It is a show-only command, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the tom object, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It appears under `show unprovisioned-inventory`, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. The AID is `unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>`, where chassis-serial-number is the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) and slot-name is the residing slot name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ), and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]`, for example `show usb-1-5-U1`; `show usb` alone lists every USB port in the node. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free storage and total-space the total storage in the associated file-system, both uint16 in MB. available-space, total-space and usb-path are only applicable when type is storage; type is either storage (file storage plus associated file management operations) or power-supply (powers external equipment such as passive shelves). present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the USB connector is inserted. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` from Operational mode. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken (see take-snapshot) before it can be activated. db-instance names the database snapshot to activate and defaults to temp. The paraphrase is a short description of the database to be activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override overrides the sanity check and takes true or false, defaulting to false. Examples: `activate-snapshot sanity-check-override` and, to activate a snapshot named onehour, `activate-snapshot onehour`. Existing snapshots can be listed first with `show database`.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after `enable-advanced-parameters` on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain your symptoms: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter has been deleted, `show advanced-parameter` reports `ERROR: object does not exist`; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but `show advanced-parameter` reports status `failed` for it. Syntax is `add|set advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>`, with `show ... [value] [status]` and `delete`. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set, unknown (default unknown). Example: `add advanced-parameter-1-4-L1-1/EEPNNLMitigation value "0 1"`.

Use `apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])` to force re-application onto TOMs that are already in place. The template-type value is serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; if no specific TOMs are provided (empty list), all system TOMs are considered. The default template-type is serdes-template. Application of serdes-templates depends on the global flag being set: `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true` (enabled/disabled, default disabled). On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively, only from that moment onward, which is why apply-template is the way to push them onto already-installed pluggables. Example: `apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1`. Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]`. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version; the confirmation therefore acts as a 'persist' trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm with `commit persist` or abandon with `commit cancel`. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands must carry the `-id=<id>` parameter, which identifies the commit confirmed, commit persist and confirmed cancel commands. All of these must be run in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with `configure`. `commit -m=<message>` attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]`, then pipe it through display commands: `show config | display commands`, and store the result for later use as a CLI script to restore the system configuration. `show config` displays only non-default configuration; anything left at its default value is skipped. The output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow it, supply an entity-id (the instance ID of the entity whose configuration you want) or, if all entities of a given type are relevant, an entity-type instead. The saved script can then be replayed, for example with `configure from-script=<script>`.

It depends on the target you pick. `configure <target>` takes exclusive or shared, and the default is exclusive: in exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration, whereas in shared mode multiple sessions can change the candidate configuration. The command runs from Operational mode and switches you into Candidate Configuration mode. You can also control the candidate's starting point: by default the Candidate Datastore starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; `from-default` starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; `from-script=<script>` imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands; `from-commit=<commit-id>` initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: `configure exclusive`.

Use `show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]`, which shows the current values of the advanced parameters that are actually running on the system, as opposed to `show advanced-parameter`, which shows what you configured plus its status. `show current-advanced-parameter` with no AID lists them all; `show current-advanced-parameter-1-7-L1-1/*` restricts the output to one optical carrier. The parameters are optical-carrier-name (string), current-advanced-parameter-name (string) and value (string, the value running on the system). The two views can differ: the guide's sample output flags a PMDEquUpdSpeed running value as not the configured value, and notes that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified since it is to be supported in a future release. Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

No, not everything. `clear [-f] database` performs a full wipe of database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system; it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; for a secure wipe or factory default use the `clear system` command instead. Three clear-type values exist, default full: full resets the database to factory defaults; keep-networking wipes the database but keeps network configurations; initialize-from-script wipes it and initializes from a pre-stored .cli script (script parameter, absolute path or filename in /storage/scripts). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user (0..64 chars) and new-admin-password, and can only be triggered by the SA user. -f forces without confirmation. Transient alarms after the controller card reboot should be ignored.

Use `db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>` from Operational mode. The type parameter defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption; encryption-with-integrity is the one that adds the integrity protection on top of encryption. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The command automatically reboots the controller, for example `db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity` enables the integrity check for the system database and reboots the controller. You can verify the result with `show db-protection-scheme`, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is noted as changeable via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm will then read hmac-sha2-512 instead of none.

Use `show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]` and read integrity-status, which indicates the status of the integrity check and takes passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled. The companion attributes are mode, the current protection scheme of the DB (encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity), which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and encryption-algorithm, xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size. On a node still in encryption-only mode the output shows integrity-algorithm none and integrity-status disabled. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run `diff [-t|-c] candidate`, which must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore and the current system configuration as created, deleted or changed objects, showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate configuration and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: plain diff style, where + is an added object or new value and - is a deleted object or old value; side-by-side table with the -t flag; as CLI commands that reproduce the candidate changes with the -c flag; and the list of commands being executed with the -d flag. So `diff -c candidate` gives you the change as commands. `diff commit <id> [<id>]` compares a commit-record with the running configuration or another commit-record, and is available only when commit-records exist (commit-tracking enabled) or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run `discard-changes`. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode, so it is only available once you have entered the candidate with `configure`. Note the scope: it throws away the entire candidate datastore, not a selected subset of edits. If instead you want to review what you staged before deciding, use `diff [-t|-c] candidate` from Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode first, and if you want to commit but keep an automatic escape hatch, use `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>]`, which rolls back to the pre-commit version if not confirmed within the timeout (default 10 minutes).

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. The commands are `add extended-config-<name>`, `delete extended-config-<name>` and `show extended-config-<name> [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Using it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side, and the name must match a name known by the system; name is a string of length 0..64. Before adding one, read its description attribute (string, length 0..255), which is provided by the system and states the description of the extended-config and its effect in the system.

Check the service-impact attribute in the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with `show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]`. service-impact identifies whether applying that parameter change causes service impact and reads service-affecting or non-service-affecting; if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock/maintenance operation or other relevant operations first. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. The same record gives supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), type, direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity (uint8, how many values you must enter). All attributes are read-only. Example: `show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/EEPNNLMitigation`.

Run `lock` from Operational mode. It locks database access to the current session and grants exclusive write access to that CLI session; it is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, any other session (CLI or another type) that tries to make a configuration receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session is already holding it. The lock is released either by the `unlock` command or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or by inactivity time-out. Only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock; unlocking a non-locked database or one locked by another session fails. After unlock, any session can configure again and take a new lock. Both commands accept only the -h help flag.

A named-value-set is addressed as `named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a value item, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The commands are `add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]`, `set ... [value <value>]`, `show ... [value]` and `delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`. All four are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Only if recovery from chassis storage is configured for it. `set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>` takes disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is needed, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the hardware), or auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the Node Controller automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service. Monitor with `show recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage] [restore-status] [backup-status] [last-backup] [next-backup]`. restore-status values are init (default), image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore; backup-status is successful, failed, in-progress or unknown.

`rollback commit [<commit-id>]` works both on the Running Datastore (the default) and on the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if the candidate is empty; that is in fact a way to initialize the candidate. So with changes already staged you must clear them first, for example with `discard-changes`. If no commit-id is given, the most recent commit-record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record and replays them in order, from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It relies on commit-records, so the commit-tracking system-policy must be enabled.

`show commit` is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither holds on your node, there are no Commit Repository records to visualize. Enable the repository with `set system-policies commit-tracking enabled` (values enabled/disabled, default disabled); note that disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The syntax is `show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]`, where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -n selects an exact number of records to obtain, and -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]` and `show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. commit-tracking (enabled/disabled, default disabled) enables the commit-repository feature: with it enabled, all configuration changes made via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back. Disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records, and the Commit Repository commands are only available while it is enabled. writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled; disabling the writable-running policy makes configuration via the running datastore impossible and forces use of the candidate: the CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 become read-only.

The db-passphrase. The system only accepts `take-snapshot` if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of the security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or locally as a parameter of the command (`take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`). The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters in accordance with the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax: `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, Operational mode. db-instance takes temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; type takes db-backup (default) or system-backup; description is a string 0..128. Re-taking an existing named snapshot overwrites the existing file.
